## Purpose

[Chapter 6](https://moderndive.com/v2/06-multiple-regression.html) in *ModernDive* extends basic regression to models with more than one explanatory variable. Multiple regression lets you look at the relationship between an outcome and one explanatory variable while *holding other variables constant*, which lets you look at averages and relationships while accounting for other variables.

In this problem set, you'll run and interpret multiple regression models with numeric and categorical explanatory variables using real data from the [V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy) project](https://www.v-dem.net/). You'll revisit two models from Problem Set 4 and see what happens to them when you account for GDP per capita. You'll also keep using the {dplyr} and {ggplot2} skills you've built so far. By the end, you should be able to:

- Use `filter()`, `drop_na()`, and `mutate()` to prepare a dataset for analysis, including rescaling a variable (like measuring GDP per capita in thousands of dollars) so that its coefficient is easier to interpret
- Calculate a correlation matrix with `select()` and `cor()` to see how an outcome is related to several explanatory variables, and how the explanatory variables are related to each other
- Use `group_by()` and `summarise()` to compare groups before running a model
- Fit a multiple regression model with `lm(y ~ x1 + x2)` and look at the results with `get_regression_table()`
- Interpret coefficients in a model with one numeric and one categorical explanatory variable, including writing out the separate equation for each group
- Visualize a model with one numeric and one categorical explanatory variable with `geom_parallel_slopes()`, and judge whether straight lines fit the data well
- Interpret partial slopes in a model with two numeric explanatory variables, making clear what is being held constant
- Interpret coefficients for a categorical variable with many categories as differences from a baseline group, holding other variables constant
- Explain why a coefficient changes (and can even flip direction) when you add another explanatory variable to a model

## Criteria for success

This problem is graded using a ✔+/✔/✔− system. I'm looking for correct code and genuine attempts at the interpretation questions, not polished prose.

- **✔+**: All chunks run without errors and use the correct functions, variables, and models. There are no warnings or messages/ The datasets, models, and plots you create match the expected output shown in the instructions. The written answers correctly interpret coefficients in plain language with the correct units *and* say what's being held constant (e.g., "among countries with the same GDP per capita, democracies have 14.5 fewer child deaths per 1,000 live births than autocracies, on average," not just "the democracy coefficient is −14.5"). Explanations for why coefficients change between models use the correlations and group averages you calculated. The extension does something new and exciting rather than only copying a previous chunk.
- **✔**: This is the expected level of performance. All chunks run and produce mostly correct results; minor mismatches (e.g., column names or rounding) are fine. Written interpretations are attempted and reasonable, though they may be missing units, forget to mention what's held constant, or mix up small details.
- **✔−**: Chunks are missing, don't run, or use the wrong variables or model (e.g., leaving out one of the explanatory variables or switching x and y in `lm()`). Written answers are left blank or only restate numbers from the output without interpreting them.

You may work together in groups of up to four, but you must turn in your own answers and note who you worked with.

And remember: **everything human-facing must be human-generated**. Don't submit AI-generated text. I want to hear *your* voice.

Also, if you do use LLMs to help with the code (I recommend not!), make sure you [follow the guidelines from the syllabus](/syllabus.qmd#rule-2-you-are-responsible-for-understanding-verifying-and-citing-everything-an-llm-generates) about how to cite what you use.
